messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
m=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor,
\]

so that

\[
m^2\le n<(m+1)^2.
\]

We need

\[
n\mid (m!)^{n!}+450.
\]

---

### 1. Prime factors of \(n\) not exceeding \(m\)

Suppose \(p^a\mid\mid n\) and \(p\le m\). Then \(p\mid m!\), so

\[
v_p\bigl((m!)^{n!}\bigr)=n!\,v_p(m!)\ge n!.
\]

Also \(a=v_p(n)\le n\), and \(n!\ge n\), so

\[
v_p\bigl((m!)^{n!}\bigr)\ge a.
\]

Thus

\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 0 \pmod{p^a}.
\]

Since \(p^a\mid n\), we must have

\[
0+(m!)^{n!}+450\equiv 450\equiv 0\pmod{p^a}.
\]

Therefore every prime power of \(n\) whose prime is \(\le m\) must divide \(450\).

---

### 2. Prime factors of \(n\) exceeding \(m\)

Suppose \(p\mid n\) and \(p>m\). Then \(p\nmid m!\). Also \(p\le n\), so \(p-1\le n\), hence

\[
p-1\mid n!.
\]

By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 1\pmod p.
\]

Since \(p\mid n\), we need

\[
1+450\equiv 0\pmod p,
\]

so

\[
p\mid 451.
\]

Factoring,

\[
451=11\cdot 41.
\]

Thus any prime factor of \(n\) exceeding \(m\) must be \(11\) or \(41\).

Also, \(n\) can have at most one prime factor greater than \(m\), because two such factors would force

\[
n\ge (m+1)^2,
\]

contradicting \(n<(m+1)^2\).

---

### 3. Bounding \(n\)

If \(n\) has no prime factor greater than \(m\), then all prime powers of \(n\) divide \(450\), so

\[
n\mid 450,
\]

and hence \(n\le 450\).

If \(n\) has exactly one prime factor greater than \(m\), call it \(q\). Then \(q\in\{11,41\}\). Write

\[
n=qs.
\]

All prime factors of \(s\) are \(\le m\), so by the first part,

\[
s\mid 450.
\]

Also \(q>m\) implies \(q^2>n=qs\), so

\[
s<q.
\]

Now check the two possibilities.

- If \(q=11\), then \(s<11\) and \(s\mid 450\). The largest such divisor is \(10\), so

\[
n\le 11\cdot 10=110.
\]

- If \(q=41\), then \(s<41\) and \(s\mid 450\). The largest divisor of \(450\) below \(41\) is \(30\), so

\[
n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

Thus every valid \(n\) satisfies

\[
n\le 1230.
\]

---

### 4. Verify that \(n=1230\) works

For \(n=1230\),

\[
m=\lfloor\sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35,
\]

and

\[
1230=30\cdot 41.
\]

Modulo \(30\): since \(30\mid 35!\) and \(30\mid 450\),

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 0\pmod{30}.
\]

Modulo \(41\): since \(\gcd(35!,41)=1\) and \(40\mid 1230!\), Fermat gives

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]

Therefore

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]

Since \(\gcd(30,41)=1\), we get

\[
1230\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

Hence the largest possible value is

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
